summary: Proposes an addition to the Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP), a way to include vendor-specific information. Comments and suggestions were sought. It was replaced by RFC 1084, RFC 1395, RFC 1497 and RFC 1533.

eli5.summary: When a computer starts up and asks for its settings, this adds extra boxes in the answer for things like helpful machines on the network.

questions: what are bootp vendor information extensions
how does bootp give configuration options
what is the bootp magic cookie
what server addresses can bootp provide
subtitle: Extra information delivered with BOOTP to help new computers configure themselves.

tldr.problem: When a computer boots and asks the network for its configuration, the BOOTP protocol needs a standard way to convey vendor-specific and site-specific information beyond just IP addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1048 defines a tagged format for a 64-octet vendor information field within BOOTP replies, using a magic cookie identifier, length-tagged subfields, and predefined tags for common server addresses and configuration data.
tldr.outcome: This version was superseded by RFC 1084, RFC 1395, RFC 1497, and RFC 1533, which provided more comprehensive BOOTP option specifications.

today: RFC 1048 was an early specification for BOOTP vendor extensions, published in February 1988. This version was superseded by RFC 1084, RFC 1395, RFC 1497, and most importantly RFC 1533, which provided more comprehensive DHCP and BOOTP option specifications that became the standard for host configuration.

sections.title: Introduction to BOOTP Configuration Extensions
sections.content:
As workstations and personal computers proliferate on the Internet, the administrative complexity of maintaining a network grows by an order of magnitude. The assignment of local network resources to each client represents a significant difficulty. Rather than delegating this responsibility to users, the solution is to define resources in uniform terms and automate their assignment.

The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) addresses the issue of assigning an IP address to a client automatically during boot, along with other resources. The basic protocol included provisions for vendor-defined resource information, but this format was not clearly specified. RFC 1048 defines a vendor-independent interpretation of this resource information, providing a standardized way for BOOTP servers to convey configuration details to booting clients.
sections.eli5: When a new computer starts up, it needs to know its settings. BOOTP is a protocol to ask a server 'What should I be configured as?' This RFC explains how to add extra information to those answers.

sections.title: BOOTP Overview and Motivation
sections.content:
While the Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) can assign an IP address to a hardware address, it provides only part of the functionality needed for automatic configuration. BOOTP is a UDP/IP-based protocol that allows a booting host to configure itself dynamically without user supervision. It provides a means to assign a host its IP address, a filename from which to download a boot program and the address of that server, and the address of an Internet gateway if present.

One obvious advantage of BOOTP is centralized management of network addresses, eliminating the need for per-host unique configuration files. In an environment with hundreds of hosts, this dramatically reduces administrative overhead. By categorizing hosts into classes and maintaining configuration information for each class, the complexity of network management is greatly reduced.
sections.eli5: BOOTP lets a computer ask a central server 'What are my settings?' instead of having someone type them in by hand. It is like calling a phone number to ask 'What should I do?' and the server tells the computer its IP address and where to find a boot program.

sections.title: Vendor Information Format and Magic Cookie
sections.content:
The BOOTP packet includes a 64-octet field reserved for vendor information, which RFC 1048 standardizes for general use. The vendor information field uses a magic cookie to identify the mode in which succeeding data should be interpreted. The magic cookie value is the 4-octet sequence 99.130.83.99 (hexadecimal: 63.82.53.63) in network byte order.

After the magic cookie, the vendor information field is implemented as free-form data with extendable tagged subfields. These subfields are length-tagged (with limited exceptions), allowing clients that do not implement certain field types to correctly skip over them. All lengths are exclusive of the tag and length octets, and all multi-byte quantities are in network byte order.
sections.eli5: The vendor information is like a set of boxes added to the BOOTP answer. Each box has a label (tag) and says how big it is, so a computer that does not understand a box can skip over it and look at the next one.

sections.title: Fixed and Variable Length Fields
sections.content:
The vendor information uses two types of fields. Fixed-length data has two formats: fields with no data consist of a single tag octet and are implicitly one octet in length, while fields with data consist of a tag octet, a length octet, and the specified number of data octets. The Pad field (tag 0) contains no data and aligns subsequent fields to word boundaries. The Subnet Mask field (tag 1) provides 4 octets specifying the subnet mask. The Time Offset field (tag 2) provides a signed 32-bit integer specifying the time offset in seconds from UTC. The End field (tag 255) marks the end of usable data.

Variable-length data fields all use the same format: tag, length, and data octets. The specification defines fields for gateway addresses (tag 3), time servers (tag 4), name servers (tags 5 and 6), log servers (tag 7), quote-of-the-day servers (tag 8), printer servers (tag 9), Impress image servers (tag 10), Resource Location Protocol servers (tag 11), and hostname (tag 12). Reserved fields (tags 128-254) are available for site-specific information.
sections.eli5: The fields are like different types of envelopes. Simple ones with fixed content (like the pad) just have a tag. Others have a tag, a size, and then that much data. Gateways and servers are lists of IP addresses, and the hostname is a text string.

sections.title: Extensibility and Registration
sections.content:
Additional generic data fields may be registered by contacting the designated administrator at USC's Information Sciences Institute. Implementation-specific use of undefined generic types (those in the range 12-127) may conflict with other implementations, so registration is required before using them. Implementation-specific fields should use the reserved range (128-254) to avoid conflicts.

When selecting information to include in the vendor-specific area, care should be taken not to exceed the 64-byte length restriction. Nonessential information such as hostname and quote-of-the-day server addresses may be excluded if needed, as these can be located using more appropriate service protocols later. The RFC notes that the multicast approach to service discovery has advantages, but acknowledges that IP multicast was not widely implemented at the time and BOOTP provides a unified discovery mechanism.
sections.eli5: If you want to add a new type of box to the vendor information, you need to register it so different computers do not use the same box for different things. There is limited space (64 bytes), so you might not fit everything you want.
